cases.title: Three distances between two hydrogel scaffolds
cases.context: In a tissue engineering lab, hydrogel scaffolds (water-swollen polymer networks on which cells are grown) were described by two features, stiffness in kilopascals (kPa) and mean pore size in micrometers (μm). The table below shows the two features for scaffold A and scaffold B. A small distance between the two scaffolds means that they are similar.
tasks: Calculate the Euclidean distance and the Manhattan distance between scaffold A and scaffold B. Make sure to show your intermediate calculations.
Calculate the Minkowski distance with p = 3 and compare all three values.
cases.symbols: \(q,r\) (two points or feature vectors), \(q_i,r_i\) (their \(i\)th coordinates), \(m\) (number of dimensions), \(p\) (Minkowski order), \(d(q,r)\) (distance).

steps.title: Coordinate differences
steps.words: Find the absolute difference for each feature first, then reuse them in every formula.

steps.title: Euclidean distance
steps.words: Square, add and take the square root.

steps.title: Manhattan distance
steps.words: Add the absolute differences.

steps.title: Minkowski distance, p = 3
steps.words: Cube, add and take the cube root.

steps.title: Compare
steps.words: Larger p puts more weight on the largest single difference, so the distance shrinks toward the largest difference, 8. The two features have different units, so in practice they would be scaled before the distance is used.

cases.conclusion: The Euclidean distance is 10, the Manhattan distance is 14, and the Minkowski distance with p = 3 is 8.99588. The features were used in their own units here, so a feature with larger numbers would count for more.
cases.source: Original practice example in the course style

cases.title: Within-cluster sums of squares for ten wound closure times
cases.context: In a study of burn care, time to wound closure (the number of days until a skin graft donor site was fully covered by new skin) was recorded for 10 patients. The 10 recorded times were 9, 10, 12, 13, 25, 27, 28, 30, 31 and 33 days. The times were clustered in R with kmeans(days, c(10, 20)). The final clusters were 9, 10, 12, 13 (centroid 11) and 25, 27, 28, 30, 31, 33 (centroid 29). The clustering was then repeated with k = 3 and k = 4. The table below shows the size (number of points in each cluster), withinss (within-cluster sum of squares) and tot.withinss (total within-cluster sum of squares) fields of the R output for each k, with k = 1 (all 10 values in one cluster) for comparison.
tasks: Calculate the within-cluster sum of squares for each of the two clusters and tot.withinss for k = 2. Calculate betweenss (between-cluster sum of squares) from the total sum of squares. Make sure to show your intermediate calculations.
Using tot.withinss for k = 1 to 4, how many clusters should be used for these times? Please state how you reached your conclusions.
cases.symbols: \(SS_j\) (within-cluster sum of squares of cluster \(j\)), \(x_i\) (entry value), \(c_j\) (centroid of cluster \(j\)), \(y_i\) (cluster label), \(k\) (number of clusters).

steps.title: Cluster 1 sum of squares
steps.words: Square each deviation from the cluster 1 centroid and add.

steps.title: Cluster 2 sum of squares
steps.words: Square each deviation from the cluster 2 centroid and add.

steps.title: Total within-cluster sum of squares
steps.words: This is tot.withinss in the R output.

steps.title: Between-cluster sum of squares
steps.words: R reports this as betweenss, 777.6. At k = 1 the whole total is within-cluster.

steps.title: Compare k = 1 to 4
steps.words: The drop from k = 1 to k = 2 is about 778. The later drops are only about 33 and 9.

steps.title: Choose k
steps.words: Beyond k = 2 there is only modest improvement, so two clusters are chosen.

cases.conclusion: withinss is 10 and 42, tot.withinss is 52, and betweenss is 777.6. tot.withinss improves only modestly for k > 2, so k = 2 is chosen. The two clusters match a group of wounds that closed in about 11 days and a group that closed in about 29 days.
cases.source: Original practice example in the course style

cases.title: Within-cluster sums of squares for weekly rescue inhaler use
cases.context: In a study of asthma control, the number of rescue inhaler puffs (doses of a quick-relief medicine taken during breathing trouble) used in one week was read from an electronic dose counter for 10 patients. The 10 recorded counts were 1, 2, 2, 3, 8, 9, 10, 16, 17 and 19 puffs. The counts were clustered in R with kmeans(puffs, c(5, 17)). The final clusters were 1, 2, 2, 3, 8, 9, 10 (centroid 5) and 16, 17, 19 (centroid 17.33333). The clustering was then repeated with k = 3 and k = 4. The table below shows the size (number of points in each cluster), withinss (within-cluster sum of squares) and tot.withinss (total within-cluster sum of squares) fields of the R output for each k, with k = 1 (all 10 values in one cluster) for comparison.
tasks: Calculate the within-cluster sum of squares for each of the two clusters and tot.withinss for k = 2. Calculate betweenss (between-cluster sum of squares) from the total sum of squares. Make sure to show your intermediate calculations.
Using tot.withinss for k = 1 to 4, how many clusters should be used for these counts? Please state how you reached your conclusions.
cases.symbols: \(SS_j\) (within-cluster sum of squares of cluster \(j\)), \(x_i\) (entry value), \(c_j\) (centroid of cluster \(j\)), \(y_i\) (cluster label), \(k\) (number of clusters).

steps.title: Cluster 1 sum of squares
steps.words: Square each deviation from the cluster 1 centroid and add.

steps.title: Cluster 2 sum of squares
steps.words: Square each deviation from the cluster 2 centroid and add. Use the unrounded centroid 52/3 to avoid rounding drift.

steps.title: Total within-cluster sum of squares
steps.words: This is tot.withinss in the R output.

steps.title: Between-cluster sum of squares
steps.words: R reports this as betweenss, 319.4333. At k = 1 the whole total is within-cluster.

steps.title: Compare k = 1 to 4
steps.words: The drop from k = 1 to k = 2 is about 319, and the drop from k = 2 to k = 3 is still about 84. The drop from k = 3 to k = 4 is only about 4.

steps.title: Choose k
steps.words: The large gain stops after k = 3, so three clusters are chosen. The k = 2 solution leaves the counts 8, 9 and 10 in the same cluster as 1 to 3, and that cluster carries most of the k = 2 sum of squares (88).

cases.conclusion: withinss is 88 and 4.66667, tot.withinss is 92.66667, and betweenss is 319.43333. tot.withinss still falls sharply from k = 2 to k = 3 and only slightly after that, so k = 3 is chosen. The three clusters match low use (1 to 3 puffs), moderate use (8 to 10 puffs) and high use (16 to 19 puffs).

cases.title: Classifying a breast lesion as benign or malignant with K = 3
cases.context: Breast lesions (lumps seen on an ultrasound scan) were described by two features, lesion size (LS) and margin irregularity (MI, how jagged the edge of the lesion looks). The data were standardized to avoid any issues associated with differences in scale; the scaled data are unitless. A new lesion that has not been biopsied has scaled values LS = 5 and MI = 4. Five lesions were scanned and then biopsied (a small tissue sample was examined under a microscope) with the following results (training set):
tasks: Without waiting for the biopsy result, classify the new lesion as Benign or Malignant. Use a K-NN classification with K = 3. Use the Euclidian distance formula for your calculations.
Make sure to show your intermediate calculations. As part of your final answer, provide the probability for the class that you chose.
cases.symbols: \(x_i\) (feature vector of training entry \(i\)), \(y_i\) (its class label), \(L\) (number of classes), \(K\) (number of nearest neighbors), \(d\) (Euclidean distance).

steps.title: Set up
steps.words: The training set has five biopsied lesions.

steps.title: Distances
steps.words: Compute the distance from the new lesion to every labeled lesion.

steps.title: Rank the distances
steps.words: Ranks are E 1, B 2, D 3, C 4, A 5, so the K = 3 nearest neighbors are E, B and D.

steps.title: Read the neighbor classes
steps.words: Lesions C and A are not neighbors, so their classes are not used.

steps.title: Classify and give the probability
steps.words: Benign is the plurality class, so the new lesion is classified as Benign.

cases.conclusion: The three nearest neighbors are E (Benign), B (Benign) and D (Malignant). The new lesion is classified as Benign. The probability that the new lesion is benign is 2/3.

cases.title: Classifying a kidney stone as uric acid or calcium oxalate with K = 3
cases.context: Kidney stones are treated differently depending on what they are made of. Computed tomography (CT) attenuation (how strongly the stone blocks X-rays, x1, in hundreds of Hounsfield units, HU) and urine pH (x2, rounded to a whole number) were recorded for patients with a stone. Stones from six patients were later removed and analyzed in the laboratory with the following results (training set):
tasks: A new patient has a stone with x1 = 6 (600 HU) and x2 = 6. Without waiting for the stone to be removed, classify the new stone as Uric acid or Calcium oxalate. Use a K-NN classification with K = 3. Use the Euclidian distance formula for your calculations.
Make sure to show your intermediate calculations. As part of your final answer, provide the probability for the class that you chose.
cases.symbols: \(x_i\) (feature vector of training entry \(i\)), \(y_i\) (its class label), \(L\) (number of classes), \(K\) (number of nearest neighbors), \(d\) (Euclidean distance).

steps.title: Set up
steps.words: The training set has six analyzed stones. The features are used in their raw units.

steps.title: Distances
steps.words: Compute the distance from the new stone to every labeled stone.

steps.title: Rank the distances
steps.words: Ranks are D 1, B 2, A 3, C 4, E 5, F 6, so the K = 3 nearest neighbors are D, B and A.

steps.title: Read the neighbor classes
steps.words: The single nearest stone, D, is calcium oxalate, but the next two, B and A, are uric acid. The other stones are not neighbors, so their classes are not used.

steps.title: Classify and give the probability
steps.words: Uric acid is the plurality class, so the new stone is classified as Uric acid.

cases.conclusion: The three nearest neighbors are D (Calcium oxalate), B (Uric acid) and A (Uric acid). The new stone is classified as Uric acid even though its single nearest neighbor is calcium oxalate. The probability that the new stone is uric acid is 2/3.

notes: All data are invented for practice. No real study, author or year is cited. No lookup is used because Session 22 has no printed critical values, so every lookup is null.
Every k-Means case is a single iteration, as in the lecture exercise. Every point is strictly closer to one initial centroid than to the other (no ties), and the check script asserts this.
No K-NN case has two equal distances. In p22-kidney-stone-knn the single nearest neighbor (D, Calcium oxalate) is outvoted by the next two (Uric acid). p22-sepsis-lactate-wbc-knn gives 3/3.

withinss tables are real R output from kmeans(). k = 2 used the starting centres named in the context. k = 1, 3 and 4 used set.seed(1) and kmeans(x, k, nstart = 50). size, withinss and tot.withinss strings are as R printed them. betweenss from R is 777.6 (wound times) and 319.4333 (inhaler puffs). The check script confirms that each table row equals the best partition for that k and that the hand algorithm run from the stated starting centres reaches the k = 2 clusters given in the context.

p22-rescue-inhaler-withinss has its elbow at k = 3, not k = 2. The hand calculation is still done for the k = 2 output, as in the lecture age example. Its starting centres c(5, 17) were chosen so that the hand algorithm (assign to the nearest centre, recompute the means) and R reach the same 7 / 3 split with no tie. From c(2, 12) the hand algorithm stops at a worse 4 / 6 split while R's default algorithm moves on to the 7 / 3 split, so that start was not used.

values keep the reference key names of each method so existing tools can read them. In the withinss cases 'ages' holds the clustered data (days or puffs). In the K-NN cases 'newMesh' holds the new object and 'pFail' holds the probability of the chosen class.
p22-hydrogel-scaffold-distance uses raw units (kPa and μm) like the lecture medicine and mesh examples. Its solution says that unscaled features let the larger-number feature count for more.

His exercise wording keeps its punctuation in context and tasks (the semicolon in 'differences in scale; the scaled data are unitless', the colons after 'initial centroids for your calculations' and 'C1', and after '(training set)'). Words, conclusions and step text have no colons or semicolons.
